title: CareThread Atlas
description: Explore a personal health record timeline by category and chronology. CareThread Atlas keeps source fields and missing-record context within reach.
attribution: The record timeline runs on FinchNode.
workflow: Filter the timeline by clinical category, reverse the chronology, and expand any event to inspect its original resource fields.
subject: Health record timeline & clinical event explorer
label: The atlas journal
headline: Building a timeline without rewriting the record
summary: A design journal about chronology, category filters and the difference between a recorded event and a complete history.
sections: CareThread Atlas arranges returned record entries into a timeline so a visitor can move through the available information. The order is a way to read the data, not a clinical narrative generated by the app. Two entries appearing next to each other do not establish a relationship or explain why an event occurred.
Change the view, preserve the entry

Visitors can filter by category, reverse chronology and expand an event to inspect its returned fields. These controls change the view rather than editing the underlying source. A narrower filter can be useful before an appointment, but it also hides other categories. The interface should be read with that selection in mind.

An imported date is whatever the returned entry supplies; it is not a license to invent a missing event time. An absent event cannot prove that care never happened. Records can arrive from different sources with different coverage, and a partial sync may leave a visible gap. The timeline preserves warnings so a clean layout does not imply a complete history.

CareThread Atlas uses a FinchNode-backed connection service. Authorization happens before record retrieval, and the timeline receives the categories granted to the visitor’s temporary session. FinchNode supplies the normalized record boundary; the atlas supplies category navigation and chronological presentation. The public code documents that separation.

The website and timeline implementation are deployed, while production connection activation is pending. This journal describes design choices in that implementation, not a patient success story. When live access is enabled, source availability will still determine which entries can be shown. The atlas is a personal review aid, not a diagnosis, a certified medical history or a replacement for a source record.
guideIntro: Follow a health-record timeline, understand date ordering and category filters, and investigate repeated entries without silently rewriting the history.
finchnodeContext: CareThread Atlas uses FinchNode’s returned record categories as material for its timeline. Ordering, filtering and expansion belong to the Atlas interface; the timeline does not manufacture missing events or decide that similar entries are duplicates.

articles.title: How to organize a health-record timeline in CareThread Atlas
articles.description: Filter health-record events by category, change chronological order and inspect the fields behind each timeline entry.

sections.heading: Choose a view of the question you are exploring
paragraphs: Start with all events to see the available record categories. Then use a category filter to focus the display on the type of entry you want to inspect. Filtering changes the visible timeline; it does not delete records or request new information from the source.

sections.heading: Check the order before reading a sequence
paragraphs: The ordering control switches between newest-first and oldest-first views. The app uses the date available on each resource. A recorded clinical date, a result date and the time something arrived in the app are not interchangeable concepts.
items: Check which category filter is selected.
Confirm the direction of the date order.
Read the source label and record ID for a relevant event.
Expand the entry before drawing a conclusion from its position.

sections.heading: Inspect entries that lack a useful date
paragraphs: An undated entry cannot establish its place in a clinical sequence just because the interface must place it somewhere. In the implementation, missing or unparseable dates use a fallback sort value. Look at the expanded object and treat the chronological position of such entries cautiously.

sections.heading: Use the timeline as an organizing view
paragraphs: The expanded entry exposes the original fields returned to this app. The timeline does not edit a provider’s chart, identify causes, or fill gaps in the history. Live record connections still await activation; the public guide explains the implemented navigation.

questions.question: Does changing the sort order update my records?
questions.answer: No. It rearranges the visible entries only.

questions.question: Why is an undated record at an edge of the timeline?
questions.answer: Entries without a parseable date use a fallback sort value. Their screen position should not be read as a confirmed event date.

articles.title: Why similar entries remain separate in a health timeline
articles.description: Learn how CareThread Atlas preserves record IDs and source context instead of automatically merging similar-looking events.

sections.heading: Similar wording can describe different records
paragraphs: Two entries can have similar labels while differing in category, date, status or source. The timeline preserves the returned entries so that a reader can inspect those differences. It does not collapse them merely because the titles look alike.

sections.heading: Inspect identity before calling something a duplicate
paragraphs: Open each event and compare its supplied fields. The displayed ID and source label provide a starting point; the expanded JSON provides more context. If the entries remain unclear, preserve the uncertainty rather than assuming that one can be discarded.

sections.heading: Presentation is not reconciliation
paragraphs: Sorting and filtering make a record easier to navigate. Deciding that two entries represent one clinical event is a different task with different evidence requirements. CareThread Atlas currently implements the navigation task and leaves source entries intact.

sections.heading: Design a future merge feature with traceability
paragraphs: An operator adding a merged view should retain access to every contributing entry and explain the matching rule. Ambiguous cases need a visible outcome. The current source implementation does not provide automatic deduplication, and these notes are not a claim that a reconciliation feature already exists.

questions.question: Does CareThread Atlas remove repeated-looking records?
questions.answer: No. It retains separate returned entries so their source fields can be inspected.

finchnode.heading: FinchNode provides categories; Atlas preserves the trail
finchnode.text: CareThread Atlas builds its timeline from the authorized categories returned through FinchNode. The product adds a category label for navigation and a chronological view while keeping the supplied record fields inspectable. That separation matters when two entries appear to describe the same thing.
finchnode.label: FinchNode’s normalized record API

articles.title: Patient timelines as a foundation for useful health AI
articles.description: CareThread Atlas examines how authorized longitudinal records can support future AI summaries while preserving dates, sources and gaps in the available history.

sections.heading: Health questions often span more than one entry
paragraphs: A person preparing to review their history may need to navigate conditions, observations, medications and encounters spread across time. A startup that sees only one isolated entry can miss the context needed even to organize the right questions. Authorized longitudinal data can make that context available, provided the interface preserves what each source actually supplied.

CareThread Atlas turns returned categories into a filterable timeline. The current product supplies navigation and expandable fields; it does not generate an account of what caused an event or reconcile the record into a single authoritative story.

sections.heading: The useful AI idea is an evidence-linked draft
paragraphs: A future assistant might draft a chronological outline, retrieve entries connected to a user’s question or group candidate discussion topics. A reader should be able to open the entries supporting each statement. That is a different design goal from producing a plausible narrative that cannot be checked.

WHO’s guidance points to opportunities for summarizing health information alongside risks from false, biased or incomplete statements. For a timeline product, that makes traceability a practical requirement for evaluating a proposed feature.

links.label: WHO guidance on generative AI applications and limitations

sections.heading: Dates can mislead a model as easily as a reader
paragraphs: A missing date does not become a known event date because software must place an item somewhere. Similar labels do not prove that two records describe the same event. A future summarizer needs access to those uncertainties, rather than receiving a flattened story in which every item appears equally certain.
items: Retain source IDs with any summary evidence.
Distinguish recorded event dates from import or sync times.
Keep undated entries visibly unresolved.
Treat repeated-looking entries as candidates for inspection, not automatic duplicates.

sections.heading: The connection choice behind the timeline
paragraphs: CareThread Atlas uses FinchNode to obtain the authorized record categories its timeline can display. Its own code adds category navigation and chronological ordering while leaving the returned fields inspectable. That gives a future AI feature an explicit boundary between retrieved evidence and newly generated language.

Current patient connection activation is still pending, and the application does not run an AI summarizer. A new operator adding one would need to decide its scope, disclosures, data handling and evaluation before enabling it.

sections.heading: Access and training are different decisions
paragraphs: Using authorized information for a visitor’s current task is not the same as retaining it for a training corpus. A startup should state which job the data serves and what happens when access ends. The opportunity is a more useful, inspectable experience for the person who shared the record, rather than an undefined accumulation of patient data.

questions.question: Does CareThread Atlas currently write AI summaries?
questions.answer: No. It filters, sorts and expands returned records. AI-supported outlines are a possible future direction described here.

questions.question: Can the timeline prove why an event happened?
questions.answer: No. Chronological ordering alone does not establish a causal relationship between clinical events.

articles.title: Best EHRs for small clinics in 2026: a ranked shortlist
articles.description: Seven EHRs ranked for independent clinics with one to ten clinicians, compared on published pricing, billing, e-prescribing and AI documentation, plus specialty picks.

sections.heading: How this shortlist was put together
paragraphs: An EHR for a small clinic has to do more than store notes. It usually carries scheduling, e-prescribing, claims, a patient portal and, increasingly, AI documentation. Switching later is expensive, so the most useful comparison is fit: who each system is designed for and what it costs to find out.

We reviewed each vendor’s own product, pricing and certification pages on September 28, 2026, alongside the 2026 Best in KLAS results for independent practices with one to ten physicians. We did not run hands-on trials. Prices are quoted only where a vendor publishes them; “quote only” means you will need a sales call.

links.label: 2026 Best in KLAS: Small Practice Ambulatory EHR/PM

sections.heading: The ranking at a glance
paragraphs: The order reflects a general independent primary care or multispecialty clinic. Specialty and cash-pay practices should read the later section before deciding.

sections.heading: 1. Elation Health — best overall for independent primary care
paragraphs: Elation is built around independent primary care, including direct primary care and pediatrics, and says more than 50,000 clinical users work in it. It won the 2026 Best in KLAS award for small-practice ambulatory EHR and practice management, its second consecutive year, with a score of 81.7.

Its pricing page lists Note Assist AI, a patient portal, telehealth and billing, but pricing is tailored. In June 2026 Elation acquired Aster, an AI-native women’s-health EHR, so expect its specialty features to widen.

sections.heading: 2. athenaOne — strongest for revenue-cycle support
paragraphs: athenaOne combines a cloud EHR with practice management and billing services, and athenahealth’s collector product won the 2026 KLAS category for independent practice management. In August 2026 athenahealth made athenaAmbient, its built-in ambient documentation, broadly available at no additional charge to athenaOne customers.
We could not confirm current pricing from athenahealth’s site, so budget for a quote. The main reason to choose it is having billing and documentation run by the same vendor.

sections.heading: 3. eClinicalWorks — the clearest published price
paragraphs: eClinicalWorks publishes its prices: $499 per provider per month for the EHR, $599 with practice management, or revenue-cycle management as a service at 2.9% of collections. It lists no start-up costs and includes training for practices of one to nine providers, along with e-prescribing, a patient portal and cloud hosting.
Its ambient scribe, Sunoh.ai, is sold separately; the Sunoh pricing page listed a limited-time price of $149 per user per month against a regular $199.

sections.heading: 4. Tebra — practice growth tools alongside the chart
paragraphs: Tebra, formed from Kareo and PatientPop, says it is purpose-built for independent practices with one to ten providers. Its EHR+ and All in One plans include e-prescribing with PDMP and EPCS support, billing, a portal and telehealth; All in One adds AI, online scheduling, review management and websites.
Pricing is quote only. Tebra raised $250 million in December 2025 to fund AI development, which suggests AI features will keep changing through 2026.

sections.heading: 5. CharmHealth — the lowest-cost way to start
paragraphs: CharmHealth has a free plan capped at 50 encounters a month, without e-prescribing or telehealth. Beyond that, you can pay $0.50 per encounter with a $25 monthly minimum, or $200 per provider per month.

Add-ons are priced individually: e-prescribing at $15 per provider per month, EPCS from $250 per provider per year, telehealth at $20 per provider per month and an AI scribe at $125 per provider per month or $2 per encounter. Add up the modules you need before comparing it with bundled systems.

sections.heading: 6. DrChrono by EverHealth — tiered bundles
paragraphs: DrChrono now sits within EverHealth and sells three quote-only tiers: Foundation, Growth and Premium. Its EverHealth Scribe is included in Premium and available as an add-on in the other tiers. Its ONC certification page lists DrChrono EHR version 11.

sections.heading: 7. Practice Fusion — simple charting, with a watch item
paragraphs: Veradigm still markets Practice Fusion to small and independent practices with e-prescribing, EPCS, billing and a free patient portal, and offers a 14-day trial. Its product page does not advertise AI documentation.
Veradigm announced a company-wide turnaround plan in September 2026. No change to Practice Fusion has been announced, but ask about the product roadmap and contract exit terms.

sections.heading: Specialty, cash-pay and larger-group picks
paragraphs: A general ranking does not fit every clinic. These systems are designed for narrower practice types.

sections.heading: Questions to ask in every demo
paragraphs: Sales demos show the best path through a product. These questions surface the costs and constraints that usually appear later.
items: Which version is ONC-certified today? Check the listing yourself on the Certified Health IT Product List.
How do we export all of our data if we leave, in what format, and at what cost?
Is EPCS included, and does e-prescribing cover every prescriber or cost extra per person?
Which clearinghouse and labs are included, and which cost extra per month?
Where is AI-drafted text stored, can we switch it off, and is it covered by the business associate agreement?
What is the contract term, the renewal notice period and the cost of migrating historical charts?

links.label: ONC Certified Health IT Product List

sections.heading: When the EHR does not cover a workflow
paragraphs: Small clinics often find gaps around the chart: a custom intake form, a post-procedure check-in or a program-specific tracker. Before adding a separate tool, ask whether your EHR vendor’s marketplace already offers it.

If you build something yourself, choose a platform that will sign a business associate agreement for patient information. Several popular AI app builders prohibit protected health information in their terms. Healthcare-focused options include Blaze, Knack Health and Caspio’s HIPAA Edition, and Panaceum, which generates HIPAA apps from a plain-language description and is currently in early access.

questions.question: Which EHR is cheapest for a solo practice?
questions.answer: Among published prices, CharmHealth’s free and per-encounter plans have the lowest entry cost, and Healthie starts at $19 a month for virtual-first practices. Add the modules you need, such as e-prescribing and billing, before comparing totals.

questions.question: Is the KLAS winner the right EHR for every small clinic?
questions.answer: No. KLAS reflects customer feedback within a segment. A therapy practice, a cash-pay clinic or a surgical specialty may be better served by a system designed for that workflow.

sections.heading: What a website for clinics needs
paragraphs: The best website development agency for a clinic should help prospective patients understand its services, meet the team and find the right appointment route. This comparison focuses on small clinics and wellness practices choosing an agency for a public-facing website, with Cider as our overall and value pick.

Start with the patient journey: services in plain language, practitioner names, office details and a clear appointment route. A first-visit page should answer practical questions without promising treatment outcomes. The website brief should distinguish public information from the systems used for records, messaging and intake.

paragraphs: Cider for Clinics explicitly targets chiropractors, physical therapists, massage therapists, acupuncturists and wellness clinics. It describes first-visit explanations, practitioner profiles and booking paths. It is our best-overall pick for a small informational practice site with an existing appointment system, rather than for a hospital platform or a custom clinical application.

Do not infer patient-data capabilities from a website-design package. Have the clinic choose its intake and portal systems, then agree how the public website routes visitors to them. For larger groups, confirm specialty content, location routing and governance in the proposal.

paragraphs: Practis focuses on healthcare marketing and lists medical website design, patient education content and patient-facing website features.
Ask which features are included in the proposed website and which are separate products. A feature listed on an agency website is not evidence that it is included in every package.

Ask for a project proposal separating design, content, development and recurring marketing. Compare the deliverables with a small launch package before comparing the headline fees.

sections.heading: What to put in your agency brief
paragraphs: Use these tasks in the proposal and the acceptance review. Ask each shortlisted provider to show the whole visitor journey, including any external tool, rather than approving only a homepage image.
items: Give a new patient a clear path from service page to the correct location and booking tool.
Ask clinicians to approve service descriptions and practitioner credentials.
Test the first-visit page with someone unfamiliar with the practice.
Document where each form sends information and who maintains it.

sections.heading: How to make the final choice

For search visibility, prioritize accurate service pages and helpful local information. Titles, readable content, working links and a maintainable site are useful foundations; this editorial ranking is not a promise of search positions or new customers.

questions.question: Can a clinic use a standard website package?
questions.answer: Often a public site can be a modest project if appointment booking and records stay in existing systems. If the project includes patient intake, messaging or record access, define those requirements separately and have the responsible team review the proposed setup.
